Technical Documentation: Configuring a Home Network Router for Parental Controls  

This document provides step-by-step guidance for configuring parental controls on a typical consumer-grade home network router. The procedures described are applicable to most modern routers—including models from major vendors such as Netgear, TP-Link, ASUS, and Linksys—that support built-in parental control features via their web-based administration interface. While specific menu labels may vary slightly by firmware version and manufacturer, the underlying configuration principles remain consistent. Users should consult their router’s user manual or vendor support portal for model-specific details prior to implementation.  

Begin by ensuring physical and logical access to the router. Connect a computer or mobile device to the local network—either wirelessly or via Ethernet—and confirm Internet connectivity. Open a web browser and enter the router’s default IP address (commonly 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1) into the address bar. Authenticate using the administrator credentials. If unchanged from factory defaults, these are often printed on the router label; however, best practice dictates that users first change the default password to prevent unauthorized access.  

Once logged in, navigate to the parental controls section. This is typically located under Settings > Security > Parental Controls or Advanced > Parental Controls, depending on the interface. Enable the parental controls feature globally before proceeding to define individual policies. Most routers require creating at least one profile per child or user group. Assign a descriptive name (e.g., “Alex – Age 10”) and associate the profile with one or more devices. Device identification can be accomplished by MAC address, device name, or DHCP client identifier. For accuracy, identify target devices by checking their network settings: on Windows, run ipconfig /all; on macOS or Linux, use ifconfig or ip addr show; on iOS or Android, inspect Wi-Fi settings. Record each device’s MAC address and enter it into the corresponding field.  

Next, configure time-based restrictions. Specify daily or weekly schedules indicating permitted online hours—for example, 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM on weekdays and 9:00 AM to 9:00 PM on weekends. Some routers support holiday-specific rules or temporary overrides, which may be enabled for special occasions. Ensure the router’s internal clock is synchronized with an NTP server; verify this under System Tools > Time Settings or similar. Incorrect time settings will cause schedule-based rules to malfunction.  

Content filtering constitutes a second critical layer. Select predefined categories (e.g., adult content, gambling, social media, gaming) to block. Note that category granularity depends on the router’s firmware and underlying filtering database. Higher-tier models may integrate third-party services such as OpenDNS Family Shield or Netgear Armor, requiring separate account registration and API key entry. Avoid relying solely on keyword blocking, as it is prone to false positives and easily circumvented. Instead, prioritize domain- and category-level enforcement. Test effectiveness by attempting to load representative sites known to fall within restricted categories.  

Application and service restrictions may also be available. These allow granular control over protocols (e.g., blocking BitTorrent traffic) or port ranges (e.g., disabling ports used by multiplayer game servers). Use such settings judiciously, as overly restrictive port blocking can interfere with legitimate services like video conferencing or cloud backups.  

After completing configuration, save all changes and reboot the router if prompted. Monitor initial behavior through the router’s activity log, accessible under Status > System Log or Monitoring > Traffic Statistics. Logs typically display blocked requests, including timestamp, source device, destination domain, and reason for denial. Review logs periodically to assess compliance and adjust policies based on observed usage patterns.  

Important considerations include privacy, reliability, and limitations. Parental controls operate at the network level and cannot govern encrypted DNS queries (e.g., DoH/DoT) unless the router itself intercepts and redirects them—a capability not universally supported. Additionally, controls apply only to traffic routed through the configured device; they do not extend to cellular data, guest networks (unless explicitly included), or devices connected via alternative upstream gateways. Finally, maintain open communication with children about digital safety practices; technical controls serve as safeguards—not substitutes—for education and shared responsibility.  

For troubleshooting, confirm that firmware is up to date, disable conflicting security software on client devices, and verify that no static IP configurations bypass DHCP-assigned profiles. Should persistent issues arise, contact the router manufacturer’s technical support with model number, firmware version, and a concise description of the observed behavior.

Western Pond Turtle (*Actinemys marmorata*)  
*Encyclopedia of North American Reptiles and Amphibians*, 3rd ed. (2023)

The western pond turtle (*Actinemys marmorata*), once abundant from southwestern British Columbia to northern Baja California, is a medium-sized freshwater chelonian distinguished by its low, keelless carapace—often olive to dark brown with faint marbling—and yellow-tinged plastron marked by irregular dark blotches. Adults reach 15–20 cm in carapace length; females are notably larger than males and exhibit broader heads and shorter tails. Unlike many North American turtles, *A. marmorata* rarely basks communally on logs or rocks—a behavior likely shaped by historical predation pressure from river otters and great blue herons. Its diet consists primarily of aquatic invertebrates, algae, and carrion, though juveniles consume proportionally more protein-rich prey.

Historically, the species occupied over 90% of suitable low-elevation wetlands across its range—including slow-moving rivers, beaver ponds, and seasonal marshes in the Willamette Valley, Central Valley of California, and Puget Sound lowlands. By the early 20th century, however, populations began collapsing. The most acute decline occurred in Oregon: surveys conducted by the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife between 1985 and 1992 documented fewer than 200 individuals remaining in the entire Willamette Basin—down from an estimated 10,000+ in the 1930s. Key drivers included habitat loss (over 95% of historic wetlands in California’s Central Valley were drained by 1970), invasive predators (notably bullfrogs (*Lithobates catesbeianus*), whose tadpoles outcompete hatchlings and whose adults consume juveniles), and road mortality during nesting migrations. A 2006 study led by Dr. Linda Trueblood at UC Davis confirmed that nest depredation by raccoons and striped skunks exceeded 85% at unprotected sites near urban corridors like Sacramento’s American River Parkway.

Conservation efforts intensified after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service listed the northwestern distinct population segment (DPS)—encompassing Washington, Oregon, and northern California—as Threatened under the Endangered Species Act in 1994. Critical habitat was designated in 2002 for 132 stream kilometers and 2,100 hectares of wetland complexes, including the Klamath River floodplain and Oregon’s Fern Ridge Reservoir. Captive head-starting programs launched at the Oregon Zoo (1999) and Woodland Park Zoo (2004) have released over 3,200 juveniles since 2000; telemetry monitoring shows post-release survival rates averaging 68% over two years—up from 22% for wild-hatched cohorts in the same habitats.

Despite these efforts, the species remains precarious. A 2022 rangewide assessment by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife recorded only 14 viable breeding populations statewide—down from 47 documented in 1988. In Washington, where the species was extirpated from the mainland by 2000, reintroductions on Protection Island (since 2015) have yielded just 17 confirmed hatchlings through 2023. Climate change poses emerging threats: prolonged droughts in California have desiccated overwintering ponds, while warming water temperatures correlate with skewed sex ratios in lab-reared clutches (a 2021 study in *Copeia* found 92% female hatchlings at constant 30°C incubation).

The western pond turtle endures—not as a relic, but as a litmus test for wetland stewardship. Its persistence hinges less on isolated reserves than on coordinated, watershed-scale restoration: reconnecting floodplains, controlling bullfrog invasions, and protecting nesting corridors from development. As conservation biologist Dr. Hector Galvan noted in his 2020 monograph *Turtles in the Crossfire*, “This turtle doesn’t ask for wilderness. It asks for functional water—and the humility to share it.”

Managing Type 2 Diabetes with Diet and Exercise

 Introduction
Living with type 2 diabetes requires a comprehensive approach to managing blood glucose levels, and diet and exercise are fundamental components of this strategy. By making informed choices about what you eat and how you move, you can significantly improve your overall health and reduce the risk of complications. This section provides practical guidance on how to integrate dietary changes and physical activity into your daily routine.

 Dietary Management

Balancing Your Plate:
A balanced diet is crucial for managing type 2 diabetes. Focus on including a variety of nutrient-dense foods that provide essential vitamins, minerals, and fiber. The following guidelines can help you make healthier food choices:

- Carbohydrates: Opt for complex carbohydrates, such as whole grains (brown rice, quinoa, oats), legumes, and non-starchy vegetables. These foods are high in fiber and have a lower glycemic index, which means they are absorbed more slowly and do not cause rapid spikes in blood sugar.
- Protein: Include lean protein sources like poultry, fish, tofu, and legumes. Protein helps to stabilize blood sugar levels and promotes satiety.
- Fats: Choose healthy fats, such as those found in avocados, nuts, seeds, and olive oil. Avoid trans fats and limit saturated fats, which are often found in processed and fried foods.
- Fruits and Vegetables: Aim for at least five servings of fruits and vegetables per day. They are rich in fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants, which are beneficial for overall health.

Portion Control:
Controlling portion sizes is key to managing blood sugar levels. Use smaller plates, measure your food, and be mindful of serving sizes. For example, a serving of cooked pasta or rice is about half a cup, and a serving of meat is about the size of a deck of cards.

Meal Planning:
Plan your meals ahead of time to avoid impulsive, unhealthy choices. Consider preparing meals in advance and packing them for work or outings. This can help you stay on track with your dietary goals.

Hydration:
Stay well-hydrated by drinking plenty of water throughout the day. Limit sugary beverages, such as soda and fruit juices, and opt for water, herbal teas, or unsweetened drinks instead.

 Exercise and Physical Activity

Benefits of Exercise:
Regular physical activity offers numerous benefits for individuals with type 2 diabetes, including improved insulin sensitivity, better blood sugar control, weight management, and reduced risk of cardiovascular disease. Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week, spread over several days.

Types of Exercise:
Incorporate a mix of different types of exercise to keep your routine engaging and effective:

- Aerobic Exercise: Activities such as brisk walking, cycling, swimming, and dancing can help improve cardiovascular health and promote weight loss.
- Strength Training: Resistance exercises, such as lifting weights or using resistance bands, build muscle mass, which can enhance insulin sensitivity and metabolic rate.
- Flexibility and Balance: Yoga and stretching exercises improve flexibility, balance, and overall mobility, reducing the risk of falls and injuries.

Getting Started:
If you are new to exercise or have been inactive for a while, start slowly and gradually increase the intensity and duration of your workouts. Consult with your healthcare provider before beginning any new exercise program, especially if you have any existing health conditions or concerns.

Staying Motivated:
Finding activities you enjoy and setting realistic goals can help you stay motivated. Consider exercising with a friend or family member, joining a fitness class, or using a fitness app to track your progress. Celebrate small victories along the way to maintain your enthusiasm and commitment.

 Conclusion
By adopting a balanced diet and regular exercise routine, you can effectively manage your type 2 diabetes and improve your quality of life. Remember to consult with your healthcare provider for personalized advice and to monitor your progress. With dedication and support, you can achieve your health goals and lead a fulfilling life.

Government Audit Report  
Office of the Inspector General  
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs  
Report No. 24-01784-12  
Date: June 15, 2024  

Subject: Oversight of Veterans’ Disability Claim Processing Times  

This report presents the findings of a comprehensive audit conducted by the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) to assess the Department of Veterans Affairs’ (VA) oversight of disability compensation claim processing times. The audit covered fiscal years 2022 and 2023 and focused on the Veterans Benefits Administration’s (VBA) performance in meeting its timeliness goals, the adequacy of internal controls, and the effectiveness of accountability mechanisms governing claim adjudication.  

The VA has publicly committed to processing initial disability claims within an average of 125 days and fully developed appeals within 135 days. However, our analysis of VBA’s national performance data reveals persistent and systemic shortfalls. Nationally, the average processing time for initial claims was 198 days in FY 2022 and 186 days in FY 2023—56 percent and 49 percent above the target, respectively. For legacy appeals, the average exceeded 420 days in both years. While some regional offices demonstrated improvement, twelve of the 57 regional processing centers reported average processing times exceeding 250 days in FY 2023. Notably, three offices—located in Muskogee, Oklahoma; St. Petersburg, Florida; and Roanoke, Virginia—consistently ranked among the slowest performers for three consecutive reporting periods.  

Our review identified several root causes undermining effective oversight. First, VBA lacks standardized, real-time metrics to identify bottlenecks at the individual claim level. Current dashboards aggregate data monthly and do not incorporate case-specific variables such as evidence development delays, medical examination scheduling gaps, or inter-agency coordination lags with the Department of Defense or Social Security Administration. Second, accountability structures remain weak. Although VBA’s Performance Management Plan includes timeliness as a strategic objective, supervisory evaluations do not systematically link timeliness outcomes to performance ratings or resource allocation decisions. We found no documented instances in FY 2022–2023 where sustained failure to meet timeliness targets resulted in corrective action, leadership review, or operational recalibration at the regional office level. Third, staffing models rely heavily on historical workload projections rather than dynamic forecasting tools. As a result, offices experiencing surges in complex claims—particularly those involving traumatic brain injury or mental health conditions—faced chronic understaffing without timely mitigation.  

We also examined VBA’s implementation of the Appeals Modernization Act (AMA) framework. While AMA introduced new appeal lanes intended to reduce backlogs, our sample review of 320 AMA appeals revealed that 41 percent experienced at least one procedural delay attributable to inconsistent application of evidence submission deadlines, unclear guidance on supplemental claims, or insufficient training for decision reviewers on newly codified standards. These inconsistencies were not routinely tracked or addressed through centralized quality assurance protocols.  

The OIG concludes that VBA’s current oversight mechanisms are insufficient to ensure consistent, transparent, and accountable management of disability claim processing timelines. Without structural reforms, veterans will continue to experience prolonged uncertainty, delayed access to essential benefits, and unnecessary financial hardship.  

We recommend that the Under Secretary for Benefits direct VBA to: (1) implement a real-time, claim-level dashboard integrated with electronic health and personnel records to enable proactive identification and resolution of delays; (2) revise the Performance Management Plan to tie supervisory accountability—including resource requests and staffing adjustments—directly to verified timeliness metrics across all claim types; (3) conduct a nationwide staffing needs assessment using predictive analytics and adjust deployment models quarterly based on validated workload indicators; and (4) establish a centralized AMA Quality Review Unit to monitor compliance, document recurring procedural deficiencies, and issue corrective guidance within ten business days of identification.  

VBA concurred with all four recommendations and provided a detailed corrective action plan, including milestones and completion dates. The OIG will monitor implementation and issue follow-up reports as warranted.  

Respectfully submitted,  
Michael T. Chen  
Inspector General  
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs

Dear Valued Shareholders,  

It’s a genuine pleasure to write this letter—not from a boardroom overlooking a skyline, but from the back room of our new Oakwood Market in Durham, North Carolina, where I spent last Tuesday unloading pallets of local honey alongside store manager Lena Patel. That small moment captures the spirit of 2023 for Harvest & Hearth: grounded, deliberate, and deeply human.  

This past year, we opened six new stores—five in underserved neighborhoods across the Southeast and one in our home state of Tennessee—and renovated eight existing locations. Our most significant milestone was the June 15 opening of the Durham store—the first full-service grocery in East Durham in over 17 years. We didn’t just build a store; we partnered with the East Durham Community Land Trust to co-develop the site, committing $2.3 million in long-term rent stabilization for adjacent affordable housing units. That decision wasn’t on any financial model—it was rooted in the conversations we had at town halls in 2022, when residents told us they wanted jobs, fresh food, and dignity—not just another chain. Today, 68% of Durham’s staff live within three miles of the store, and our local vendor program there sources 42% of produce, dairy, and baked goods from farms and producers within 90 miles.  

Revenue grew 12.4% to $418.7 million—slightly ahead of our guidance—but what matters more is *how* that growth landed. Gross margin improved to 26.8%, up 40 basis points, driven by reduced spoilage (down 19% year-over-year) and stronger private-label penetration: our “Hearth Pantry” line now accounts for 18.3% of total sales, up from 14.1% in 2022. That’s not just shelf space—it’s trust. When customers choose our organic lentils or house-roasted coffee, they’re voting for values they see reflected in our sourcing, wages, and community investment. Speaking of wages: in January, we raised our minimum hourly wage to $18.50 across all stores—$2.25 above the regional median—and launched our first-ever tuition reimbursement program, already supporting 37 team members pursuing degrees in nutrition, supply chain management, and social work.  

We also made hard choices. In October, we closed our two oldest stores—in Jackson, TN and Columbia, SC—after careful review. Neither met our updated standards for refrigeration efficiency, accessibility, or community integration. Rather than patch them, we redirected $5.2 million into modernizing our distribution center in Murfreesboro, which now handles 92% of our own deliveries (up from 74% in 2022), cutting last-mile emissions by 28%.  

None of this happens without you. Your continued confidence—evidenced by the 94% shareholder vote in favor of our 2023 ESG resolution—gave us the runway to invest where others pull back. And your patience as we navigated a 14-week labor negotiation with UFCW Local 1170? That mattered deeply. The resulting contract included profit-sharing tied to store-level food waste reduction targets—a first in our industry.  

Looking ahead, we’re not chasing scale for its own sake. In 2024, we’ll open three more stores—including one in rural Greene County, AL, scheduled for August—and launch our first mobile market unit to serve seniors in low-access ZIP codes. We’ll also publish our first third-party audited impact report, measuring everything from kilowatt-hours saved per square foot to meals donated through our “Hearth Table” program (1.2 million served in 2023).  

Thank you—for believing that a grocery store can be both profitable and purposeful. For showing up—not just as investors, but as neighbors, parents, and advocates. I’ll be at the ribbon-cutting in Greene County this summer. Hope to see you there.  

Warmly,  
Elena Ruiz  
CEO & Co-Founder  
Harvest & Hearth Regional Grocers

text:
Managing Type 2 Diabetes with Diet and Exercise

Introduction

Type 2 diabetes is a chronic condition characterized by high blood sugar levels, which can lead to serious health complications if not managed effectively. While medication may be necessary for some individuals, lifestyle modifications, particularly in the areas of diet and exercise, play a crucial role in controlling blood glucose levels and improving overall health. This section provides guidance on how to manage type 2 diabetes through these essential lifestyle changes.

Dietary Recommendations

A balanced and nutritious diet is fundamental in managing type 2 diabetes. The goal is to maintain stable blood glucose levels, achieve or maintain a healthy weight, and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. Here are some key dietary principles to follow:

1. Carbohydrate Management:
   - Carbohydrates have the most significant impact on blood glucose levels. Focus on consuming complex carbohydrates, such as whole grains, legumes, and vegetables, which are digested more slowly and provide a steady release of glucose.
   - Limit your intake of simple carbohydrates, such as white bread, sugary drinks, and sweets, as they can cause rapid spikes in blood sugar.

2. Fiber Intake:
   - Increase your fiber intake by including plenty of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains in your diet. Fiber helps slow the absorption of sugar into the bloodstream, promoting better blood glucose control.

3. Healthy Fats:
   - Incorporate healthy fats, such as those found in avocados, nuts, seeds, and olive oil. These fats are beneficial for heart health and can help you feel full, reducing the likelihood of overeating.
   - Avoid trans fats and limit saturated fats, which are often found in processed and fried foods, as they can contribute to heart disease.

4. Protein:
   - Include lean protein sources, such as fish, poultry, tofu, and legumes, in your meals. Protein is important for maintaining muscle mass and can help regulate appetite.

5. Portion Control:
   - Pay attention to portion sizes to avoid overconsumption of calories. Use smaller plates, measure your food, and be mindful of hunger and fullness cues.

6. Hydration:
   - Drink plenty of water throughout the day. Water is essential for overall health and can help prevent dehydration, which can affect blood glucose levels.

7. Meal Planning:
   - Plan your meals in advance to ensure a balanced and varied diet. Consider working with a registered dietitian to develop a personalized meal plan that meets your specific needs and preferences.

Exercise Recommendations

Regular physical activity is another critical component of managing type 2 diabetes. Exercise helps improve insulin sensitivity, lower blood glucose levels, and promote weight loss. Follow these guidelines to incorporate exercise into your routine:

1. Aerobic Exercise:
   - Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming. You can break this down into shorter sessions, such as 30 minutes five days a week.
   - If you prefer, you can also engage in 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week, such as running or high-impact aerobics.

2. Strength Training:
   - Include strength training exercises, such as weightlifting or resistance band workouts, at least two days a week. Strength training helps build muscle, which can improve insulin sensitivity and overall metabolic health.

3. Flexibility and Balance:
   - Incorporate flexibility and balance exercises, such as yoga or tai chi, to enhance your overall physical well-being and reduce the risk of falls.

4. Consistency:
   - Make exercise a regular part of your daily routine. Consistency is key to reaping the benefits of physical activity. Find activities you enjoy to increase your likelihood of sticking with them.

5. Blood Glucose Monitoring:
   - Monitor your blood glucose levels before, during, and after exercise, especially if you are new to an exercise regimen or if you are taking insulin. Exercise can lower blood glucose levels, so it’s important to be aware of any changes and adjust your treatment plan accordingly.

6. Consult Your Healthcare Provider:
   - Before starting a new exercise program, consult with your healthcare provider to ensure it is safe for you. They can provide personalized recommendations based on your current health status and any potential risks.

Conclusion

By making informed choices about your diet and engaging in regular physical activity, you can effectively manage type 2 diabetes and improve your overall quality of life. Remember to work closely with your healthcare team to develop a comprehensive management plan that addresses your individual needs and goals. With dedication and support, you can take control of your diabetes and live a healthier, more active life.

text:
The proposed offshore wind farm off the coast of New Jersey represents a significant step toward achieving the state’s legally mandated goal of 100% clean energy by 2035 and its broader climate commitments under the Global Warming Response Act. Located approximately 15 to 40 nautical miles east of Atlantic City in federal waters of the Outer Continental Shelf, the project would consist of up to 120 wind turbines, each with a maximum hub height of 160 meters and rotor diameters exceeding 220 meters, generating up to 1.2 gigawatts of electricity—enough to power over 500,000 homes annually. While the project offers substantial benefits in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and advancing energy resilience, it also poses measurable environmental risks that require careful mitigation, monitoring, and adaptive management.

Construction activities—including site characterization, cable laying, foundation installation (primarily monopile or jacket structures), and turbine erection—are expected to span 24 to 36 months. These phases will generate underwater noise, particularly during pile driving, which may temporarily displace or injure marine mammals and fish, especially sensitive species such as North Atlantic right whales, fin whales, and harbor porpoises. To address this, the project must implement strict marine mammal observation protocols, real-time passive acoustic monitoring, soft-start procedures, and seasonal restrictions on high-noise activities during peak migration and calving periods. The U.S. National Marine Fisheries Service has required a formal Incidental Take Authorization, and adherence to all stipulated mitigation measures is essential to avoid population-level impacts.

Operational effects include potential collision risks for birds and bats, particularly during nocturnal migration across the Mid-Atlantic Flyway. Pre-construction avian and bat surveys indicate moderate use of the area by migratory songbirds, shorebirds, and raptors; however, no known major concentrations of endangered avian species occur directly within the project footprint. Radar-based shutdown systems, lighting modifications compliant with FAA and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service guidance, and ongoing post-construction monitoring will be employed to minimize avian mortality. Cumulative effects from multiple offshore wind projects along the East Coast are also being evaluated regionally through the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management’s Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement.

Benthic habitat disruption is another key concern. Installation of foundations and inter-array and export cables will disturb seabed sediments and alter local benthic communities. While much of the proposed lease area consists of sandy substrates with relatively low benthic diversity, localized impacts on hard-bottom habitats and associated species—including black sea bass, summer flounder, and juvenile lobsters—must be assessed. Cable burial depth standards (minimum 1.5 meters below seabed) and avoidance of known reef complexes or sensitive benthic areas help reduce long-term harm. Notably, turbine foundations may eventually function as artificial reefs, potentially enhancing local fish abundance over time—a possible net ecological benefit requiring long-term study.

Electromagnetic fields (EMFs) from subsea transmission cables could affect electroreceptive species such as elasmobranchs (sharks and skates) and certain flatfish. Modeling indicates EMF levels drop rapidly with distance and remain well below thresholds known to cause behavioral or physiological disruption at typical exposure distances. Nevertheless, cable routing avoids known nursery grounds and migratory corridors where feasible, and future monitoring will track movement patterns of tagged species near operational infrastructure.

Socioeconomic and cumulative considerations include impacts on commercial and recreational fisheries, vessel traffic, and visual resources. Coordination with the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council and state fishery agencies has led to compensatory measures including gear loss reimbursement, temporary access restrictions with advance notice, and funding for fishery-independent research. Visual impacts from shore are minimal due to distance and prevailing atmospheric conditions, though some residents report concerns about horizon line alteration; these are largely aesthetic rather than environmental.

In conclusion, the proposed offshore wind farm presents a net environmental benefit when weighed against the continued reliance on fossil-fueled generation. Its contribution to decarbonizing the regional grid—avoiding an estimated 2.4 million metric tons of CO₂-equivalent emissions annually—significantly outweighs localized, mitigable impacts. Continued transparency, rigorous enforcement of mitigation commitments, adaptive management based on monitoring data, and robust stakeholder engagement—including Tribal consultation and input from fishing communities—are critical to ensuring responsible development. With diligent oversight and science-informed adaptation, the project can serve as a model for sustainable offshore renewable energy deployment along the U.S. Atlantic coast.

U.S. DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE  
OFFICE OF INSPECTOR GENERAL  
AUDIT REPORT NO. OIG-24-017-ARC  
*Date Issued: June 12, 2024*  

Audit of the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) Program – Phase I Implementation in West Virginia  

Between October 2022 and May 2024, OIG audited the administration of the $578 million BEAD allocation to West Virginia—funded under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA). Our review focused on project timelines, cost controls, and oversight mechanisms used by the West Virginia Broadband Office (WVBO), led by Director Sarah Linh, and its prime contractor, SummitConnect Solutions LLC (based in Charleston, WV).  

The program’s original implementation schedule—approved by NTIA on March 15, 2023—required completion of all engineering design work by December 31, 2023, with construction initiation no later than March 31, 2024. As of May 31, 2024, only 19 of 42 funded projects had completed design; the remaining 23 remain in “design limbo,” averaging 142 days past deadline. The most delayed project—the Greenbrier County Fiber-to-the-Premises rollout—was scheduled for design sign-off on November 10, 2023. It was not approved until April 22, 2024—a 163-day delay directly attributable to three rounds of rework demanded by WVBO after SummitConnect submitted technically compliant plans.  

Cost overruns are equally acute. WVBO reported total obligated funds of $211.4 million as of May 31, 2024. However, our analysis of invoices, change orders, and internal WVBO cost-tracking logs revealed $18.7 million in unapproved or unsupported expenditures—nearly 9% of obligations. Of that amount, $7.3 million stems from SummitConnect’s repeated use of non-competitive subcontractor selections for civil engineering services, violating both NTIA’s Procurement Standards (§ 200.318) and WVBO’s own Project Oversight Manual (Rev. 2.1, dated August 2022). One subcontractor, Triad Geospatial Inc., billed $1.2 million for right-of-way surveys across Boone and Logan Counties—despite having performed identical work for a prior WVBO pilot in 2021 at 42% lower cost. No price reasonableness analysis was documented.  

We also identified systemic weaknesses in progress reporting. WVBO’s monthly performance reports to NTIA consistently overstated construction readiness. For example, its March 2024 submission claimed “92% of projects have secured utility pole attachment agreements.” Our field verification found only 51% had fully executed, signed agreements; the remainder consisted of unsigned MOUs or draft letters of intent. When confronted, Deputy Director Marcus Bell acknowledged the mischaracterization during our April 17 interview but attributed it to “staff bandwidth constraints”—a claim contradicted by WVBO’s HR records showing two full-time procurement analysts were reassigned to internal IT upgrades between January and April 2024.  

NTIA guidance requires states to submit quarterly risk registers. WVBO’s first such register, submitted April 1, 2024, omitted five known high-risk issues—including labor shortages in southern counties and unresolved zoning disputes in Mercer County—until we flagged them during our site visit to Princeton on April 25.  

This is not an isolated failure of execution—it reflects a breakdown in governance. WVBO lacks a standing technical review board; SummitConnect’s sole quality assurance officer resigned in December 2023 and remained unfilled until April 2024. Meanwhile, NTIA’s regional office conducted only one in-person oversight visit between October 2023 and May 2024—on February 6, 2024—during which staff did not review any design packages or subcontractor documentation.  

We recommend that NTIA withhold the next $42.5 million disbursement to West Virginia pending certification from WVBO that: (1) all overdue design packages are closed within 30 days; (2) SummitConnect’s subcontracting practices undergo third-party audit; and (3) a qualified, independent technical reviewer is embedded full-time at WVBO by July 15, 2024. Absent corrective action, West Virginia risks forfeiting up to $112 million in remaining BEAD funds—and more critically, delays broadband access to over 43,000 unserved households beyond the IIJA’s statutory deadlines.  

Signed,  
*Elena R. Torres*  
Assistant Inspector General for Audit  
U.S. Department of Commerce  
June 12, 2024

text:
The University of Northfield today announced the official launch of the Centre for Advanced Battery Innovation (CABI), a multidisciplinary research hub dedicated to accelerating the development, commercialisation, and sustainable deployment of next-generation energy storage technologies. Located on the university’s newly expanded Science and Engineering Campus, CABI brings together over 45 faculty researchers, postdoctoral fellows, graduate students, and industry partners to tackle critical challenges in battery performance, safety, longevity, recyclability, and equitable access.

Funded through a combination of $28 million in federal research grants, $12 million in private-sector commitments, and $7 million in university seed investment, the centre represents one of the largest academic initiatives of its kind in the region. Its establishment follows a three-year feasibility study conducted by the university’s Energy Futures Task Force, which identified battery technology as a pivotal enabler of national decarbonisation goals, grid resilience, electric mobility, and global energy equity.

CABI will pursue four core research thrusts: first, solid-state and sodium-ion battery systems designed to replace scarce or geopolitically sensitive materials like cobalt and lithium with abundant, low-cost alternatives; second, AI-driven battery management and predictive analytics to extend operational life and improve real-time safety monitoring; third, closed-loop recycling processes that recover over 95% of critical cathode metals using low-energy, water-based chemistry—eliminating the need for high-temperature smelting; and fourth, community-integrated energy storage pilots that co-design modular battery systems with rural and underserved communities to support microgrids, renewable integration, and emergency power resilience.

“The battery is no longer just a component—it’s infrastructure,” said Dr. Elena Torres, founding Director of CABI and Professor of Materials Engineering. “Our work goes beyond incremental improvements. We’re rethinking batteries from the atom up—from raw material sourcing and manufacturing ethics to end-of-life stewardship and local impact. This isn’t just about higher energy density. It’s about building systems that are safer, fairer, and truly sustainable across their entire lifecycle.”

The centre’s physical infrastructure includes state-of-the-art electrochemical testing suites, dry-room battery cell fabrication labs, advanced microscopy and spectroscopy facilities, and a dedicated pilot-scale recycling line capable of processing 200 kg of spent batteries per week. All laboratories meet ISO 14644-1 Class 5 cleanroom standards and are equipped with real-time emissions monitoring and solvent recovery systems to ensure environmental compliance and occupational safety.

CABI has already secured collaborative agreements with eight industrial partners—including three Tier-1 automotive suppliers, two grid-scale energy storage developers, and three cleantech startups—each contributing co-funding, testbed access, and workforce training pathways. Notably, the centre has embedded a dual-track education programme: a new undergraduate minor in Sustainable Energy Storage launching this autumn, and a professional certificate in Battery Systems Integration open to engineers, policymakers, and utility professionals nationwide.

In alignment with the university’s commitment to inclusive innovation, CABI has launched the Battery Equity Fellowship, offering full scholarships, mentorship, and paid research placements to students from historically underrepresented backgrounds in STEM. The fellowship prioritises applicants from communities disproportionately affected by legacy mining practices and fossil fuel infrastructure.

University President Dr. Marcus Lin stated, “This centre reflects our belief that world-class research must be anchored in responsibility and relevance. CABI doesn’t exist in isolation—it’s a living collaboration between science, policy, industry, and community. Its success will be measured not only in patents and publications but in kilowatt-hours stored cleanly, jobs created locally, and batteries responsibly retired and reborn.”

CABI will host its inaugural public symposium on 14 October, featuring keynote addresses from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Electricity, representatives from the International Council on Clean Transportation, and community leaders from the Appalachian Energy Justice Coalition. The centre is now accepting proposals for its first round of seed grants, with applications due 30 November. Manchester City Football Club has been fined £100,000 by the English Football League (EFL) following a pitch invasion by supporters during their Championship fixture against Sheffield Wednesday on Saturday, 13 April. The incident occurred in the 89th minute at Hillsborough Stadium, prompting immediate intervention from stewards and police, and leading to the temporary suspension of play.

According to an official EFL statement released on Monday, the sanction follows a formal investigation into breaches of Regulation 30.1 — which prohibits unauthorised entry onto the playing surface — and Regulation 32.1, concerning spectator conduct likely to bring the game into disrepute. The governing body confirmed that footage reviewed by its Regulatory Commission showed approximately 15–20 fans entering the field without permission after Manchester City’s second goal sealed a 3–1 victory.

The match, played before a crowd of 36,412, had been largely peaceful until the final stages. However, as players celebrated the decisive goal, a group of supporters surged past perimeter barriers near the South Stand. Stewards attempted to contain the breach, but several individuals reached the centre circle before being escorted off by security personnel. Play was halted for six minutes while officials assessed safety conditions. No injuries were reported, though two individuals were arrested on suspicion of trespass and are currently assisting police with their inquiries.

In its written ruling, the EFL noted that while Manchester City had implemented “a robust pre-match security plan”, including additional stewarding resources and enhanced perimeter monitoring, the club bore ultimate responsibility for the conduct of its supporters under the terms of its membership agreement. The commission acknowledged mitigating factors — including the club’s prompt cooperation with investigators and its longstanding record of compliance — but stressed that pitch invasions represent a serious threat to player welfare, match integrity, and broader public confidence in the sport.

Manchester City issued a formal apology late Sunday evening. In a statement posted on its official website, Chief Executive Officer Omar Berrada said: “We unequivocally condemn the actions of those individuals who entered the pitch. Such behaviour is unacceptable, dangerous, and wholly inconsistent with the values we uphold as a club. We fully accept the EFL’s decision and will work closely with authorities to reinforce preventative measures ahead of future away fixtures.”

The club confirmed it has launched an internal review of its away-fan protocols, including the use of facial recognition technology at designated travel hubs and stricter accreditation procedures for supporter groups. It also announced plans to introduce mandatory educational briefings for all registered away supporters, focusing on stadium safety regulations and consequences of misconduct.

This is not the first time Manchester City has faced disciplinary action related to fan conduct this season. In February, the club received a formal warning after pyrotechnics were discharged during an FA Cup tie at Wembley. However, the current fine marks the largest financial penalty imposed on the club for spectator-related breaches since its promotion to the Championship in 2022.

Football governance experts caution that such incidents reflect wider challenges facing English football amid rising attendances and heightened emotional intensity. Dr Helen Carter, Senior Lecturer in Sports Law at Loughborough University, observed: “Pitch invasions are rare in the professional game, but when they occur, they test the limits of existing crowd management frameworks. Clubs must balance fan engagement with uncompromising safety standards — and regulators must ensure sanctions are both proportionate and deterrent.”

The EFL reiterated that further breaches could result in more severe penalties, including stadium bans or points deductions, particularly if evidence emerges of organised or premeditated conduct. Its statement concluded: “The integrity of the competition depends on respect for the rules — by players, officials, and spectators alike. This decision sends a clear message: no individual, however passionate, stands above the law of the game.”

Manchester City’s next away fixture is scheduled for 27 April at Stoke City’s bet365 Stadium. Security arrangements for that match are understood to be under active review by both club and local authorities.

text:
This grant proposal outlines a community oral-history project to be led by the Maplewood Public Library, in partnership with local schools, senior centers, and cultural organizations. The project will collect, preserve, and share the lived experiences of longtime residents—particularly those from historically underrepresented groups including Black, Latino, Indigenous, immigrant, and LGBTQ+ communities—to strengthen intergenerational connection, deepen civic engagement, and enrich the library’s role as a trusted community archive.

Maplewood is a midsize city undergoing rapid demographic and economic change. While its public library serves over 20,000 patrons annually, many long-standing residents feel their stories are absent from official narratives—whether in school curricula, municipal planning documents, or local media. Existing historical collections at the library reflect only a narrow slice of the community’s past: predominantly white, English-speaking, middle-class perspectives. This gap not only erases vital contributions but also limits opportunities for youth to see themselves reflected in local history—and for new residents to understand the layered roots of the place they now call home.

Over twelve months, the library will train 25 community volunteers—including high school students, retirees, and bilingual adults—in ethical oral-history methods: active listening, trauma-informed interviewing, consent protocols, and basic audio recording. Training will be co-facilitated by professional oral historians from the state historical society and staff from the university’s Center for Community Memory. Each volunteer will conduct three to five interviews (totaling at least 75 recorded oral histories), prioritizing elders, longtime small-business owners, labor organizers, educators, and others whose firsthand accounts illuminate pivotal moments: neighborhood desegregation efforts in the 1960s, the impact of factory closures in the 1980s, refugee resettlement initiatives since the 1990s, and grassroots responses to recent climate-related flooding.

All interviews will be conducted in participants’ preferred language and setting—homes, community centers, or quiet library rooms—with full informed consent and clear rights agreements. Recordings will be professionally digitized, transcribed (with participant review), and archived in the library’s newly established Local Voices Digital Repository—a publicly accessible, searchable online platform built on open-source software and compliant with accessibility standards (WCAG 2.1). Each transcript will include contextual notes, relevant photographs (with permission), and links to related archival materials. No interview will be published without explicit, written permission; participants retain copyright and may request redaction or withdrawal at any time.

The project extends beyond documentation. A series of free public programs will bring stories to life: “Story Circles” where youth and elders co-create short audio pieces; bilingual storytelling festivals at neighborhood parks; and curriculum-aligned lesson plans distributed to all district middle and high schools. Teachers will receive training to integrate oral histories into social studies and English classes, fostering critical thinking about source analysis, narrative authority, and historical empathy. Additionally, the library will host a traveling exhibit—featuring portraits, audio clips, and quotes—displayed first at the main branch, then rotating through branch libraries, senior centers, and local businesses.

Sustainability is central to the design. Volunteers will form an ongoing Oral History Collective, supported by library staff, to steward future projects. Staff will receive internal training to maintain the digital repository and continue outreach. Evaluation will be participatory: quarterly feedback sessions with volunteers and participants, pre- and post-project surveys measuring shifts in perceived community belonging and historical awareness, and analysis of digital platform usage and program attendance. Success will be measured not only by number of interviews collected but by depth of engagement—e.g., 80% of participants report feeling “seen and heard,” 60% of student volunteers express increased interest in local civic issues, and at least five community organizations adopt oral-history methods in their own work.

The total budget request is $72,500, covering personnel (project coordinator, part-time archivist, interpreter stipends), equipment (recorders, microphones, backup drives), transcription services, digital platform development and hosting, training materials, honoraria for community narrators ($50 per interview), and outreach supplies. The library commits $15,000 in matching funds—including staff time, meeting space, and existing technology—and has secured letters of support from the Maplewood School District, the ElderCare Alliance, the Latinx Cultural Council, and the City’s Office of Equity and Inclusion.

This project affirms that history is not static—it is spoken, shared, contested, and renewed. By placing storytelling tools in community hands and ensuring equitable access to the resulting archive, the Maplewood Public Library will help cultivate a more inclusive, resilient, and historically grounded community—one voice at a time.

title: legal memorandum|whether a non-compete clause is enforceable under state law
text:
MEMORANDUM  

TO: Partner  
FROM: Associate  
DATE: April 5, 2024  
SUBJECT: Enforceability of Non-Compete Clauses Under State Law  

This memorandum addresses the enforceability of non-compete clauses under applicable state law. Because non-compete agreements are governed exclusively by state law—and because standards vary significantly across jurisdictions—this analysis focuses on the prevailing legal framework in states that follow the traditional reasonableness doctrine, such as New York, Massachusetts, and Illinois, while also noting recent legislative developments, particularly in states with heightened restrictions (e.g., California, Oklahoma, and more recently, Minnesota and Washington).  

Under common law principles adopted in most jurisdictions, a non-compete clause is enforceable only if it satisfies a three-part reasonableness test: (1) it is no greater in scope than necessary to protect a legitimate business interest; (2) it does not impose an undue hardship on the employee; and (3) it is not injurious to the public interest. Courts apply this test strictly and construe ambiguities against the drafter—typically the employer. Legitimate business interests generally include protection of trade secrets, confidential information, goodwill, and substantial customer relationships developed through the employee’s tenure. Mere prevention of ordinary competition or retention of trained personnel, absent additional factors, is insufficient.  

Geographic and temporal limitations are critical to judicial assessment. A restriction confined to counties where the employee actually worked or solicited clients—and lasting no longer than twelve to twenty-four months—is often upheld for mid- to senior-level employees. In contrast, nationwide bans or durations exceeding two years face strong judicial skepticism, especially for non-managerial staff. Similarly, overbroad prohibitions—such as barring employment with any competitor regardless of role, industry segment, or function—are routinely invalidated. Courts increasingly require tailoring: e.g., prohibiting work with direct competitors in the same product line within a defined region, rather than blanket industry-wide bans.  

Recent statutory developments have materially altered the landscape. California Business and Professions Code § 16600 renders nearly all post-employment non-competes void, with narrow exceptions for certain equity sales and dissolution agreements. Oklahoma and North Dakota have enacted similarly sweeping prohibitions. Effective July 1, 2023, Minnesota prohibits non-competes for employees earning at or below the median state income; Washington limits enforceability to employees earning above 100% of the state’s median income and mandates advance written notice. Most notably, the Federal Trade Commission issued a final rule on April 23, 2024, banning most non-compete clauses nationwide—but that rule is currently subject to preliminary injunctions and its enforceability remains uncertain pending judicial review. Until resolved, state law remains the controlling authority.  

Courts also examine procedural fairness. Agreements presented on a “take-it-or-leave-it” basis to existing employees generally require new, independent consideration—such as a promotion, bonus, or severance enhancement—to be enforceable. Mere continuation of at-will employment is insufficient in many jurisdictions, including Pennsylvania and Texas. Additionally, some states, like Maine and Rhode Island, mandate specific disclosures or waiting periods before execution. Failure to comply with such formalities may render the clause void ab initio.  

In summary, enforceability turns on careful drafting and contextual application. A narrowly tailored non-compete—limited in duration, geography, and scope; supported by adequate consideration; and designed solely to safeguard identifiable, legitimate interests—has a reasonable prospect of enforcement in most moderate-jurisdiction courts. However, boilerplate provisions, overreaching restrictions, or agreements imposed without meaningful negotiation or additional consideration carry substantial risk of invalidation. Counsel should therefore advise clients to conduct jurisdiction-specific reviews prior to implementation, consider alternatives such as non-solicitation or confidentiality agreements where appropriate, and ensure compliance with both substantive and procedural statutory requirements.  

Respectfully submitted,  
Associate

Species Profile: Spiny Softshell Turtle (Apalone spinifera)

The Spiny Softshell Turtle, *Apalone spinifera*, is a freshwater species known for its distinctive appearance and unique adaptations. Native to North America, this turtle is found in a variety of aquatic habitats, including rivers, lakes, and marshes, from southern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico. The species was first described by Charles Alexandre Lesueur in 1827, and it has since been the subject of numerous studies due to its ecological significance and conservation concerns.

Physical Characteristics

The Spiny Softshell Turtle is easily recognizable by its flat, leathery carapace, which lacks the bony scutes typical of most other turtles. Instead, the carapace is covered with a flexible, rubbery skin that allows for greater agility and speed in water. Adult females can reach lengths of up to 19 inches (48 cm), while males are generally smaller, averaging around 7 inches (18 cm). The name "spiny" refers to the small, pointed projections along the leading edge of the carapace, particularly noticeable in young individuals. The turtle's snout is long and tubular, an adaptation that aids in breathing while submerged and in capturing prey.

Habitat and Distribution

*Apalone spinifera* is widely distributed across the central and eastern United States, as well as parts of southern Canada. Its range extends from New York and Pennsylvania westward to Minnesota, and southward to Florida and Texas. This species prefers clear, sandy-bottomed waters, where it can bury itself in the substrate to avoid predators and regulate its body temperature. It is also common in areas with abundant vegetation, which provides cover and food sources.

Behavior and Ecology

Spiny Softshell Turtles are primarily carnivorous, feeding on a diet that includes fish, insects, crayfish, and mollusks. They are active hunters, using their sharp jaws to capture and tear apart prey. These turtles are known for their strong swimming abilities, with webbed feet and a streamlined body that allow them to move quickly through the water. During the breeding season, which typically occurs in late spring and early summer, females lay clutches of 10 to 30 eggs in sandy nesting sites. The incubation period lasts approximately 2 to 3 months, after which the hatchlings emerge and make their way to the water.

Conservation Status

The Spiny Softshell Turtle faces several threats that have led to declines in some populations. Habitat loss and degradation, pollution, and overharvesting for the pet trade are among the primary concerns. Additionally, the construction of dams and other barriers can disrupt the natural flow of rivers, affecting the turtles' ability to move between habitats and find suitable nesting sites. As a result, the species is listed as "Least Concern" on the IUCN Red List, but certain local populations are considered vulnerable or threatened.

In 2021, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service initiated a review of the status of the Eastern Spiny Softshell Turtle (*A. s. spinifera*), a subspecies found in the northeastern United States. This review aims to assess the current population trends and determine whether the subspecies warrants protection under the Endangered Species Act. Conservation efforts, such as habitat restoration, nest protection, and public education, are crucial for the long-term survival of this species.

Conclusion

The Spiny Softshell Turtle, *Apalone spinifera*, is a remarkable freshwater species with a rich natural history and a vital role in its ecosystem. While it remains relatively widespread, the ongoing threats to its habitat and populations highlight the need for continued monitoring and conservation efforts. By protecting the rivers, lakes, and marshes that these turtles call home, we can ensure that future generations will continue to enjoy the presence of this fascinating creature.

Subject: Audit of Delays and Cost Overruns in the Federal Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) Program  

This report presents findings from an audit conducted between October 2023 and April 2024 to assess the management and implementation of the BEAD Program, a $42.5 billion federal initiative administered by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) to expand high-speed internet access in unserved and underserved communities. The audit focused on project execution timelines, cost controls, oversight mechanisms, and compliance with statutory and regulatory requirements. Fieldwork included reviews of 42 state and territorial broadband plans, analysis of 117 funded subgrants totaling $3.8 billion, interviews with NTIA staff, state broadband office personnel, and selected subgrantees, and site visits to 12 deployment locations across eight states.

The audit identified systemic delays and significant cost overruns across multiple tiers of the program. As of March 31, 2024, only 39 percent of awarded BEAD funds had been obligated, and just 12 percent had been expended. More critically, 68 percent of reviewed subgrants were operating behind schedule—averaging 14.2 months beyond their original completion dates. Fourteen subgrants—representing $412 million in federal awards—had experienced delays exceeding two years. Primary causes included inadequate pre-award feasibility assessments, protracted permitting processes at local and tribal levels, insufficient right-of-way coordination, and unanticipated environmental and geological challenges not accounted for during planning.

Cost overruns were equally pervasive. Of the 117 subgrants examined, 89 (76 percent) reported final budget increases ranging from 9 to 47 percent above initial award amounts. Aggregate additional costs totaled $528 million, or approximately 13.8 percent of the reviewed award value. These overruns stemmed largely from scope changes necessitated by revised engineering designs, escalation in fiber optic cable and labor costs—exceeding inflation projections by 22 percent—and unplanned mitigation measures for historic preservation and wildlife habitat protections. Notably, 31 subgrants lacked formal change-order documentation or prior NTIA approval for budget adjustments, indicating weaknesses in financial controls and compliance monitoring.

The audit further found that NTIA’s oversight framework was insufficient to detect or mitigate these issues in a timely manner. While the agency established performance milestones and quarterly reporting requirements, its review process relied heavily on self-reported data without independent verification. NTIA did not conduct comprehensive risk assessments for high-value subgrants prior to award, nor did it mandate third-party engineering validation for technical plans. Additionally, state broadband offices—the primary intermediaries—lacked standardized training, staffing capacity, and authority to enforce contractual remedies, contributing to inconsistent accountability.

These deficiencies pose material risks to the program’s statutory objectives, including the requirement to achieve universal broadband access by 2030. Prolonged delays impede economic development, telehealth delivery, and remote education in targeted communities. Unchecked cost growth threatens the sustainability of remaining funding allocations and may necessitate reallocation from higher-need areas to cover overruns elsewhere.

We recommend that NTIA: (1) require rigorous, independently validated feasibility studies and risk-adjusted cost modeling for all future subgrants; (2) strengthen pre-award reviews to include mandatory right-of-way and permitting readiness assessments; (3) implement real-time financial and schedule tracking with automated alerts for variances exceeding five percent; (4) issue clear guidance on permissible scope changes and enforce strict adherence to change-order protocols; and (5) establish a dedicated capacity-building fund to support state and tribal broadband offices in technical, legal, and fiscal oversight functions.

NTIA concurred with all recommendations and has outlined a corrective action plan to be implemented by December 2024. The Office of the Inspector General will monitor progress and conduct a follow-up review in Q2 FY2025.

Respectfully submitted,  
Michael T. Reynolds  
Inspector General  
U.S. Department of Commerce

Bill Summary: H.R. 2345 - Small Business Apprenticeship Tax Credit Expansion Act of 2023

Sponsor: Representative Sarah Thompson (D-CA)

Introduced: July 15, 2023

Committee: House Committee on Ways and Means

Summary:

The Small Business Apprenticeship Tax Credit Expansion Act of 2023, introduced by Representative Sarah Thompson (D-CA) on July 15, 2023, aims to provide significant financial incentives for small businesses that hire and train apprentices. The bill seeks to address the growing skills gap in the American workforce by encouraging small businesses to invest in the next generation of skilled workers.

Key Provisions:

1. Tax Credit Increase:
   - The bill proposes to increase the existing tax credit for small businesses that hire apprentices from $1,500 to $3,000 per apprentice. This increase is designed to offset the costs associated with training and mentoring new employees.
   - For small businesses that hire apprentices from underrepresented communities, including minorities, women, and individuals with disabilities, the tax credit would be further increased to $4,500 per apprentice.

2. Eligibility Requirements:
   - To qualify for the tax credit, small businesses must have fewer than 100 employees and must register their apprenticeship programs with the U.S. Department of Labor.
   - The apprenticeship program must meet the standards set by the Department of Labor, including structured on-the-job training, related technical instruction, and a written agreement between the employer and the apprentice.

3. Duration and Limitations:
   - The enhanced tax credits would be available for a period of five years, starting from the date of the bill's enactment.
   - The total amount of tax credits a small business can claim in a single tax year is capped at $50,000, ensuring that the benefits are spread across a wide range of small businesses.

4. Reporting and Accountability:
   - Businesses receiving the tax credit will be required to submit an annual report to the Department of Labor, detailing the number of apprentices hired, the duration of their training, and the outcomes of the apprenticeship program.
   - The Department of Labor will conduct periodic audits to ensure compliance with the program's requirements and to evaluate the effectiveness of the tax credit in promoting apprenticeships.

Funding and Budget Impact:
- The bill is estimated to cost approximately $500 million over the five-year period, according to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO). The funding will be allocated from the general revenue fund.
- The CBO also projects that the expansion of the tax credit will result in a net positive economic impact, as it will lead to an increase in skilled labor and potentially reduce unemployment rates in the long term.

Support and Opposition:
- The bill has garnered support from various industry groups, labor unions, and small business associations, who see it as a crucial step in addressing the skills gap and fostering economic growth.
- Some fiscal conservatives have expressed concerns about the cost and potential for abuse, but the bill includes robust oversight measures to mitigate these risks.

Conclusion:
The Small Business Apprenticeship Tax Credit Expansion Act of 2023 represents a strategic investment in the future of the American workforce. By providing substantial financial incentives for small businesses to hire and train apprentices, the bill aims to create a more skilled and diverse labor force, ultimately benefiting both employers and employees. As the bill moves through the legislative process, it is expected to receive broad bipartisan support and could become a key component of the nation's workforce development strategy.

text:
Section 3: Managing Type 2 Diabetes Through Diet and Physical Activity  
*Evidence-based, practical, and grounded in current clinical guidelines (NICE NG28, ADA Standards of Care 2024, and SIGN 154)*  

Diet and physical activity are not adjuncts to treatment for type 2 diabetes—they are foundational, first-line interventions with proven efficacy in improving glycaemic control, reducing cardiovascular risk, preserving beta-cell function, and, in many cases, enabling sustained remission. Unlike pharmacological approaches, lifestyle modification addresses the underlying pathophysiology: insulin resistance and progressive decline in insulin secretion. When implemented consistently and supported by healthcare professionals, these changes yield measurable, clinically meaningful benefits—often within weeks.

Nutrition: Prioritising Quality, Consistency, and Individualisation  
There is no single “diabetes diet.” Instead, evidence supports a pattern of eating that emphasises whole, minimally processed foods, appropriate portion sizes, and consistent carbohydrate distribution across meals. The primary nutritional goals are:  
- To achieve and maintain a healthy body weight (a 5–10% weight loss confers significant metabolic benefit in overweight or obese individuals);  
- To improve insulin sensitivity through dietary composition;  
- To prevent postprandial hyperglycaemia without increasing hypoglycaemia risk;  
- To reduce atherogenic dyslipidaemia and blood pressure.  

Carbohydrates remain central to meal planning—not because they must be restricted indiscriminately, but because their *type*, *amount*, and *timing* directly influence glucose response. Prioritise complex carbohydrates rich in viscous fibre: oats, legumes, barley, non-starchy vegetables, and whole fruits (e.g., berries, apples, pears). These slow gastric emptying and blunt post-meal glucose excursions. Limit refined grains, sugary beverages, and ultra-processed snacks—these contribute disproportionately to glycaemic volatility and caloric excess.  

Protein intake should be moderate (15–20% of total energy), sourced from lean meats, fish, eggs, tofu, lentils, and low-fat dairy. Evidence does not support high-protein diets for long-term glycaemic or renal outcomes in people without established kidney disease. Fat quality matters more than quantity: replace saturated fats (butter, fatty meats, palm oil) with unsaturated fats (olive oil, avocados, nuts, oily fish). Omega-3 fatty acids from marine sources may modestly improve triglyceride levels but do not significantly alter HbA1c.  

Meal timing and structure matter. Skipping meals—particularly breakfast—can exacerbate insulin resistance and increase compensatory hunger later in the day. Regular, balanced meals spaced no more than 4–5 hours apart help stabilise glucose and support adherence. Use of the “plate method” offers a practical, visual guide: fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables (e.g., broccoli, spinach, peppers), one-quarter with lean protein, and one-quarter with whole-grain or starchy vegetables (e.g., quinoa, sweet potato, lentils). Avoid rigid calorie counting unless clinically indicated; focus instead on food quality, satiety cues, and sustainable habits.

Physical Activity: Dose, Type, and Integration into Daily Life  
Physical activity improves insulin sensitivity within hours of completion—a transient but potent effect that accumulates with regularity. The goal is not athletic performance, but consistent movement that becomes habitual. Current guidelines recommend:  
- At least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (e.g., brisk walking, cycling, swimming), spread over at least three days, with no more than two consecutive days without activity;  
- Resistance training at least twice weekly, targeting all major muscle groups (legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders, arms);  
- Reduction of prolonged sedentary time—break sitting every 30 minutes with 2–3 minutes of light activity (e.g., standing, gentle stretching, walking).

Moderate intensity means you can talk but not sing comfortably. Resistance training need not require gym equipment: bodyweight exercises (squats, lunges, push-ups), resistance bands, or household items (e.g., water bottles as weights) are effective. Crucially, even modest increases in activity yield benefit: adding just 2,000 steps per day (≈1 km) is associated with a 0.1–0.2% reduction in HbA1c over six months.  

Safety considerations are essential. Individuals with peripheral neuropathy should wear well-fitted, cushioned footwear and inspect feet daily. Those with proliferative retinopathy should avoid activities involving heavy lifting, straining, or rapid head movements. Always consult your GP or diabetes team before initiating a new exercise regimen—particularly if you have cardiovascular disease, autonomic neuropathy, or unstable glycaemia.

Sustaining Change: Beyond Willpower  
Behavioural sustainability hinges on realistic goal-setting, structured support, and compassionate self-monitoring. Set SMART goals (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound)—for example, “Walk for 15 minutes after dinner on four evenings this week,” rather than “Exercise more.” Self-monitoring of blood glucose may be useful during initial dietary adjustment or when starting new activity, but it is not routinely required for all. Focus instead on objective markers: waist circumference, energy levels, sleep quality, and how clothing fits.  

Remember: setbacks are expected and informative—not failures. A single high-glucose reading or missed walk does not negate weeks of progress. Work with your diabetes care team to interpret patterns, troubleshoot barriers (e.g., time constraints, emotional eating, fatigue), and adjust strategies collaboratively. Lifestyle management is lifelong, iterative, and deeply personal. It is not about perfection—but about persistent, purposeful engagement with your health.

Flooding Forces Hundreds of Families from Their Homes in Welsh Valley  

By Rhian Davies, BBC Wales Correspondent  
12 April 2024  

Torrential rainfall over the past 72 hours has triggered severe flooding across the Upper Towy Valley in Carmarthenshire, forcing more than 350 people from their homes and prompting a major emergency response. Roads have been submerged, bridges isolated, and essential services disrupted in what local authorities describe as the worst flooding event in the area for over a decade.  

The River Towy, which winds through the rural communities of Llandeilo, Ffairfach, and Dyffryn Cennen, rose rapidly after sustained downpours delivered over 120 millimetres of rain—nearly double the average April total—in less than two days. The Environment Agency issued a Severe Flood Warning for the valley early yesterday morning, its highest alert level, advising residents to evacuate immediately.  

Emergency services worked through the night deploying high-water vehicles and inflatable boats to reach stranded households. Fire crews from Swansea, Neath Port Talbot, and Powys joined forces with local mountain rescue teams and volunteers from the Welsh Air Ambulance’s ground support unit. Over 60 personnel were involved in the overnight operation, rescuing at least 47 individuals—including several elderly residents and young children—from properties cut off by fast-flowing water.  

“We’ve never seen the river behave like this in living memory,” said Elin Morgan, a lifelong resident of Ffairfach whose home was evacuated at 2:15am. “The water came up so fast—within an hour, it was lapping at our front door step. We grabbed passports, medication, and our cat, and left everything else behind.”  

Local schools—including Ysgol Gymraeg Bro Myrddin in Llandeilo—have been repurposed as emergency rest centres. More than 280 people are currently accommodated there and at community halls in nearby villages, with Red Cross volunteers providing hot meals, blankets, and psychological first aid. NHS Wales has deployed mobile health units to assess vulnerable residents, while GPs and mental health professionals are offering on-site support.  

Transport infrastructure has suffered extensive damage. The A4069—a key route connecting the valley to Llandovery—remains closed in both directions near the Cwmdu Bridge after floodwaters undermined its foundations. Network Rail confirmed that the Heart of Wales Line is suspended between Llandeilo and Llandovery due to track inundation and debris accumulation. Bus operators have introduced temporary shuttle services, but many rural roads remain impassable.  

Carmarthenshire County Council declared a local major incident late yesterday, activating its civil contingency plan. Council leader Emlyn Jones said: “This is not just about water levels—it’s about livelihoods, heritage, and community resilience. Farms have lost livestock, small businesses face weeks of closure, and historic buildings—including parts of the 13th-century Dinefwr Castle estate—are at risk from prolonged saturation.”  

Environment Agency hydrologists caution that further heavy rain is forecast for midweek, raising concerns about renewed pressure on already saturated ground. “Soil moisture deficits are critically low across south-west Wales,” explained Dr. Gareth Hughes, Senior Hydrological Adviser. “Even moderate rainfall now could trigger rapid runoff and flash flooding in tributary streams feeding into the Towy.”  

The Welsh Government has dispatched Emergency Response Co-ordinator Sian Gwenllian to the area and pledged immediate financial support. First Minister Mark Drakeford visited affected communities this morning, stating: “Our priority is safety and stability—not just in the coming days, but in the months ahead. We will ensure every family receives the support they need to recover, rebuild, and return home safely.”  

Meanwhile, residents are beginning the slow process of assessing damage. In Dyffryn Cennen, volunteer groups have formed clean-up brigades, assisted by Welsh Water engineers who are working around the clock to restore supply and prevent contamination. “We’re neighbours first,” said volunteer coordinator Owain Griffiths. “When your barn floods or your shop gets ruined, you don’t wait for permission—you roll up your sleeves and help.”  

The Met Office has maintained its amber weather warning for rain across southern Wales until Thursday evening. Authorities urge residents to avoid unnecessary travel and to monitor official updates via Floodline, the Welsh Government’s emergency portal, and local radio stations.  

As dusk falls over the valley, the sound of generators hums alongside the steady rush of the swollen river—a reminder of nature’s power, and of the quiet determination taking hold among those who call this landscape home.
